question: Which of the following is an example of a heterogeneous mixture?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Sand and water.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Sand and water form a heterogeneous mixture, because the two components remain physically distinct and the composition is not uniform throughout. The sand can be seen separately and settles at the bottom. (विषमांगी मिश्रण)

 

• A heterogeneous mixture has visible boundaries of separation between its constituents, and they can generally be separated by simple physical means such as filtration, sedimentation and decantation.

 

• A homogeneous mixture, by contrast, has a uniform composition throughout and no visible boundaries — a solution is the standard example.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Methods of separating mixtures, frequently asked in SSC:
◦ Filtration — insoluble solid from a liquid (sand from water)
◦ Evaporation — soluble solid from a liquid (salt from sea water)
◦ Sublimation — a sublimable solid from a non-sublimable one (camphor from sand)
◦ Distillation — two miscible liquids with different boiling points
◦ Chromatography — coloured components of a dye or ink
◦ Centrifugation — cream from milk
◦ Magnetic separation — iron filings from sulphur
◦ Separating funnel — two immiscible liquids (oil and water)

 

NOTE

 

• Air (Option 1): A homogeneous mixture of gases, chiefly nitrogen (78%) and oxygen (21%).

 

• Brass (Option 2): An alloy of copper and zinc, and therefore a homogeneous mixture.

 

• Sugar dissolved in water (Option 3): A solution, the classic example of a homogeneous mixture.

question: Which of the following was the first bank to be established in India?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Bank of Hindustan.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Bank of Hindustan, established at Calcutta in 1770, was the first bank in India. It was set up by the agency house of Alexander and Company and was wound up in 1832. (बैंक ऑफ हिंदुस्तान — 1770, भारत का पहला बैंक)

 

• The three Presidency Banks followed:
◦ Bank of Bengal (1806)
◦ Bank of Bombay (1840)
◦ Bank of Madras (1843)

 

• These three were amalgamated in 1921 to form the Imperial Bank of India, which was nationalised in 1955 on the recommendation of the Gorwala Committee and renamed the State Bank of India.

 

• The first bank with entirely Indian capital and management was the Punjab National Bank, founded in 1894 at Lahore, with Lala Lajpat Rai among its founders. The Allahabad Bank (1865) is the oldest joint-stock bank in India to have survived under the same name for a long period.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Reserve Bank of India was established on 1 April 1935 on the recommendation of the Hilton Young Commission (1926), and was nationalised on 1 January 1949. Its first Governor was Sir Osborne Smith and its first Indian Governor C.D. Deshmukh.

 

• Fourteen banks were nationalised in 1969 and six more in 1980. New Bank of India was merged with Punjab National Bank in 1993.

 

NOTE

 

• Punjab National Bank (Option 1): Founded in 1894; the first bank run wholly by Indian capital, but not the first bank in the country.

 

• Bank of Bengal (Option 2): Established in 1806, the first of the three Presidency Banks, but not the first bank in India.

 

• Imperial Bank of India (Option 3): Formed in 1921 by merging the three Presidency Banks.

question:
Which of the following statements is/are correct regarding human blood groups?

I. Blood group O is known as the universal donor.

II. Blood group AB is known as the universal recipient.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Both I and II.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Both statements are correct. (रक्त समूह O — सर्वदाता; AB — सर्वग्राही)

 

• Statement I is correct: blood group O is the universal donor, because its red blood cells carry neither the A nor the B antigen, and so are not attacked by the antibodies present in the plasma of any recipient. Strictly, it is O negative that is the true universal donor.

 

• Statement II is correct: blood group AB is the universal recipient, because its plasma contains neither anti-A nor anti-B antibodies, and so it can receive blood of any group. Strictly, it is AB positive that is the true universal recipient.

 

• The ABO blood group system was discovered by Karl Landsteiner in 1901, for which he received the Nobel Prize in 1930. The Rh factor was discovered by Landsteiner and Wiener and is named after the rhesus monkey.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Antigens and antibodies in the four groups:
◦ Group A — antigen A, antibody anti-B
◦ Group B — antigen B, antibody anti-A
◦ Group AB — antigens A and B, no antibodies
◦ Group O — no antigens, both anti-A and anti-B antibodies

 

• Erythroblastosis foetalis occurs when an Rh-negative mother carries an Rh-positive foetus in a subsequent pregnancy.

 

• An adult has about 5 to 6 litres of blood; blood is about 55% plasma and 45% cells. The spleen is called the graveyard of RBCs.

 

NOTE

 

• Options 1, 2 and 4 are incorrect, because both the given statements are factually accurate.

question: In Indian philosophy, the concept of 'Moksha' refers to ______.
option_1: the lawful acquisition of wealth and material prosperity
option_2: the fulfilment of legitimate desires and enjoyment
option_3: liberation from the cycle of birth, death and rebirth
option_4: the performance of prescribed ritual sacrifices
solution_text:
The correct answer is liberation from the cycle of birth, death and rebirth.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Moksha means liberation or release from the cycle of birth, death and rebirth (samsara), and is regarded as the highest and final aim of human life. (मोक्ष — जन्म-मृत्यु के चक्र से मुक्ति)

 

• It is the last of the four Purusharthas, the aims of human life:
◦ Dharma — righteousness, moral duty and law
◦ Artha — the lawful acquisition of wealth and material well-being
◦ Kama — desire, pleasure and legitimate enjoyment
◦ Moksha — liberation, the final release

 

• In Buddhism the corresponding state is called Nirvana, and in Jainism Kaivalya. The doctrine of Karma governs the cycle of rebirth, and moksha is release from that cycle.

 

• The paths to moksha described in the Bhagavad Gita are Jnana Yoga (knowledge), Bhakti Yoga (devotion) and Karma Yoga (selfless action).

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The six orthodox (astika) schools of Indian philosophy are Samkhya, Yoga, Nyaya, Vaisheshika, Mimamsa and Vedanta, and each offers its own account of the means to moksha.

 

• The four Ashramas, or stages of life, are Brahmacharya (studentship), Grihastha (household life), Vanaprastha (retirement) and Sannyasa (renunciation), the last being directed wholly towards moksha.

 

NOTE

 

• Option 1 describes Artha, the second Purushartha.

 

• Option 2 describes Kama, the third Purushartha.

 

• Option 4 describes Yajna, the ritual sacrifice central to the Vedic religion, which is a means rather than an aim of life.

question: 'Mardani Khel', a traditional armed martial art, is associated with which Indian state?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Maharashtra.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Mardani Khel is a traditional armed martial art of Maharashtra, developed by the Marathas and closely associated with the reign of Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj. (मर्दानी खेल — महाराष्ट्र)

 

• It is practised chiefly in the Kolhapur region and makes use of weapons such as the dandpatta (a gauntlet sword), the talwar, the lathi and the vita. It was suited to the hilly terrain of the Sahyadris and to rapid guerrilla fighting.

 

• The name derives from *mard*, meaning a brave man; historically the art was practised by women as well, and Rani Lakshmibai is traditionally said to have been trained in it.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Traditional martial arts of India, frequently asked in SSC:
◦ Kalaripayattu — Kerala; regarded as one of the oldest martial arts in the world
◦ Silambam — Tamil Nadu; a stick-fighting art
◦ Thang Ta and Sarit Sarak — Manipur
◦ Gatka — Punjab; associated with the Sikhs
◦ Cheibi Gad-ga — Manipur
◦ Thoda — Himachal Pradesh; involves archery
◦ Musti Yuddha — Varanasi, Uttar Pradesh
◦ Inbuan Wrestling — Mizoram
◦ Mallakhamb — Maharashtra; a gymnastic art performed on a pole or rope

 

• Velakali of Kerala and Paika Akhada of Odisha are martial dance forms rather than fighting arts.

 

NOTE

 

• Rajasthan (Option 1): Known for the Ghoomar and Kalbelia dances.

 

• Gujarat (Option 2): Known for folk forms such as Garba and Dandiya Raas rather than for a martial art of this kind.

 

• Punjab (Option 4): Home of Gatka, a distinct Sikh martial art using the stick and sword.

question: The 'Bastar Dussehra' of Chhattisgarh, regarded as the longest Dussehra festival in the world, is celebrated for approximately how many days?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 75 days.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Bastar Dussehra, celebrated in the Bastar region of Chhattisgarh, continues for about 75 days, which makes it the longest Dussehra festival in the world. (बस्तर दशहरा — लगभग 75 दिन)

 

• It is unusual in that it is not connected with the Ramayana at all. It is dedicated to the local deity Danteshwari Devi, the presiding goddess of the Bastar royal family, and there is no burning of Ravana's effigy.

 

• The festival is believed to have been begun in the fifteenth century by the Kakatiya ruler Purushottam Deo. Its principal rituals include Pat Jatra (the worship of wood), Deri Gadhai, Kalash Sthapana, Jogi Bithai, Rath Parichalan (the pulling of the great wooden chariot) and Muria Darbar, an assembly of tribal headmen.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Other festivals of Chhattisgarh: Madai, Bhoramdeo Mahotsav, Hareli, Pola, Champaran Mela and Rajim Kumbh (Rajim Maghi Punni Mela).

 

• Distinctive regional forms of Dussehra elsewhere: Mysore Dasara in Karnataka, famous for the Jamboo Savari elephant procession; Kullu Dussehra in Himachal Pradesh, which begins on the day Dussehra ends elsewhere; and the Ramlila of Ramnagar in Varanasi, inscribed on the UNESCO list of Intangible Cultural Heritage.

 

NOTE

 

• 25 days (Option 1), 50 days (Option 2) and 100 days (Option 4) are incorrect. The figure to remember is 75 days, beginning around Hareli Amavasya in the month of Shravan and ending well after Vijayadashami.

question: Why does a passenger standing in a moving bus fall forward when the bus stops suddenly?
option_1: Because of the inertia of rest
option_2: Because of the inertia of motion
option_3: Because of the gravitational pull of the Earth
option_4: Because of the centrifugal force acting on him
solution_text:
The correct answer is Because of the inertia of motion.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• When a moving bus stops suddenly, the passenger falls forward because of the inertia of motion. (गति का जड़त्व)

 

• The reason is that the lower part of his body, being in contact with the floor of the bus, stops along with the bus, while the upper part continues to remain in motion on account of inertia. The upper body is therefore thrown forward.

 

• Inertia is the tendency of a body to resist any change in its state of rest or of uniform motion. It is described by Newton's First Law of Motion, also called the Law of Inertia, and is measured by the mass of the body — the greater the mass, the greater the inertia.

 

• The three kinds of inertia:
◦ Inertia of rest — a passenger falls backward when a stationary bus starts suddenly
◦ Inertia of motion — a passenger falls forward when a moving bus stops suddenly
◦ Inertia of direction — a passenger leans outward when a bus turns a corner sharply

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Other everyday illustrations of inertia: dust is removed from a carpet by beating it; a coin placed on a card over a glass falls into the glass when the card is flicked away; fruit falls from a tree when the branch is shaken; and an athlete runs some distance before a long jump.

 

• Newton's Second Law gives F = ma, and the Third Law states that to every action there is an equal and opposite reaction, which explains the recoil of a gun and the working of a rocket.

 

NOTE

 

• Option 1 is incorrect — the inertia of rest explains the opposite case, in which a passenger falls backward when a bus starts suddenly.

 

• Option 3 is incorrect — gravity acts vertically downward and does not throw the body forward.

 

• Option 4 is incorrect — the centrifugal force is a pseudo force experienced during circular motion, not during sudden braking.

question: The Diwani rights of Bengal, Bihar and Odisha were granted to the East India Company by the Treaty of Allahabad, concluded after which battle?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Battle of Buxar.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Battle of Buxar was fought on 22 October 1764 between the forces of the East India Company under Hector Munro and the combined armies of Mir Qasim (Nawab of Bengal), Shuja-ud-Daula (Nawab of Awadh) and Shah Alam II (the Mughal Emperor). (बक्सर का युद्ध — 1764)

 

• It was followed by the Treaty of Allahabad, 1765, concluded by Robert Clive, under which:
◦ The Company obtained the Diwani rights — the right to collect revenue — of Bengal, Bihar and Odisha from Shah Alam II, in return for an annual payment of 26 lakh rupees.
◦ Awadh was restored to Shuja-ud-Daula on payment of a war indemnity, and became a buffer state.

 

• This grant established the Dual System of Government in Bengal, under which the Company held the Diwani (revenue) and the Nawab retained the Nizamat (administration and justice) — a division of power from responsibility that led to the terrible Bengal Famine of 1770. The dual system was abolished by Warren Hastings in 1772.

 

• Buxar is regarded as more decisive than Plassey, because it established the Company's authority not merely over Bengal but over the Mughal Emperor himself.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Battle of Plassey (1757) was fought between Robert Clive and Siraj-ud-Daula, and was won largely through the treachery of Mir Jafar. It laid the political foundation of British rule in India.

 

• The Regulating Act of 1773 was the first step by the British Parliament to control the Company's affairs; it made Warren Hastings the first Governor-General of Bengal.

 

NOTE

 

• Battle of Plassey (Option 1): Fought in 1757; it gave the Company political influence in Bengal but not the Diwani.

 

• Battle of Wandiwash (Option 3): Fought in 1760 between the English and the French during the Third Carnatic War, and it ended French ambitions in India.

 

• Third Battle of Panipat (Option 4): Fought in 1761 between the Marathas and Ahmad Shah Abdali, and had no connection with the Diwani.

question: The Indian Institute of Science (IISc), Bengaluru, was established in which year?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1909.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Indian Institute of Science (IISc) at Bengaluru was established in 1909, and began teaching in 1911. (भारतीय विज्ञान संस्थान — 1909)

 

• It was founded through the vision and endowment of Jamsetji Nusserwanji Tata, with the support of the Maharaja of Mysore, Krishnaraja Wadiyar IV, who granted land, and of the Government of India. It is therefore often called the "Tata Institute".

 

• Sir Morris Travers was its first Director. Sir C.V. Raman served as its first Indian Director, from 1933, and Homi J. Bhabha, Vikram Sarabhai and Satish Dhawan were all associated with it.

 

• IISc was granted the status of an Institution of Eminence and is consistently ranked among India's leading research institutions.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Years of establishment of other major Indian scientific and educational institutions:
◦ Indian Association for the Cultivation of Science, Kolkata — 1876, founded by Mahendralal Sircar
◦ Council of Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR) — 1942
◦ Tata Institute of Fundamental Research (TIFR), Mumbai — 1945, founded by Homi Bhabha
◦ IIT Kharagpur, the first IIT — 1951
◦ Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC) — 1954, as the Atomic Energy Establishment, Trombay
◦ ISRO — 1969
◦ Indian Institute of Space Science and Technology (IIST), Thiruvananthapuram — 2007, Asia's first space university

 

NOTE

 

• 1899 (Option 1) is the year in which Jamsetji Tata's proposal was first considered, but the institute itself was vested in 1909.

 

• 1919 (Option 3) and 1929 (Option 4) do not correspond to the founding of IISc.

question: Under the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (MGNREGA), what proportion of the wage employment is required to be given to women?
solution_text:
The correct answer is At least one-third.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Under MGNREGA, at least one-third (33%) of the beneficiaries must be women who have registered and requested work. (मनरेगा — कम से कम एक-तिहाई महिलाएँ)

 

• The Act was passed in 2005 as the National Rural Employment Guarantee Act and renamed after Mahatma Gandhi in 2009. It came into force on 2 February 2006, first in 200 districts, beginning at Bandlapalli in Anantapur district, Andhra Pradesh.

 

• Its principal provisions:
◦ A legal guarantee of 100 days of unskilled manual wage employment in a financial year to every rural household whose adult members volunteer for it
◦ Work to be provided within 15 days of application, failing which an unemployment allowance is payable
◦ Work to be provided within 5 km of the applicant's village, or an extra 10% wage if beyond
◦ Social audit by the Gram Sabha, and the Gram Panchayat as the principal implementing authority

 

• It is administered by the Ministry of Rural Development and is the world's largest employment guarantee programme, based on a rights-based, demand-driven approach.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• MGNREGA is a step towards implementing the Directive Principle in Article 41, which requires the State to secure the right to work within the limits of its economic capacity.

 

• Other major rural schemes: PMAY-Gramin, PMGSY (rural roads), DAY-NRLM (livelihoods), Jal Jeevan Mission and SVAMITVA.

 

NOTE

 

• At least one-fourth (Option 1), two-fifths (Option 3) and one-half (Option 4) are incorrect. The statutory figure is one-third, and it is worth noting that in practice the participation of women has generally been well above this minimum.

question: The splitting of white light into its constituent colours on passing through a glass prism is called ______.
solution_text:
The correct answer is dispersion.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Dispersion is the splitting of white light into its seven constituent colours on passing through a prism. (प्रकाश का वर्ण-विक्षेपण)

 

• The band of colours so obtained is called the spectrum, and the sequence is remembered by the mnemonic VIBGYOR — Violet, Indigo, Blue, Green, Yellow, Orange, Red.

 

• The cause is that different colours have different wavelengths and therefore travel at different speeds in glass, so each is refracted through a different angle. Violet has the shortest wavelength and is bent the most; red has the longest wavelength and is bent the least.

 

• The phenomenon was first studied systematically by Sir Isaac Newton, who used a second inverted prism to recombine the colours into white light and so proved that white light is composite.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• A rainbow is a natural spectrum formed by the dispersion, internal reflection and refraction of sunlight by water droplets suspended in the atmosphere. It is always seen in the direction opposite to the Sun.

 

• Related optical phenomena frequently asked:
◦ Scattering of light — explains the blue colour of the sky and the red colour of the Sun at sunrise and sunset (Rayleigh scattering)
◦ Tyndall effect — the scattering of light by colloidal particles, seen when sunlight passes through the canopy of a dense forest or through a smoke-filled room
◦ Total internal reflection — explains the working of optical fibres, the sparkle of a diamond and the appearance of a mirage
◦ Refraction — explains why a stick appears bent in water and why a coin in a bowl of water appears raised

 

NOTE

 

• Reflection (Option 1): The bouncing back of light from a surface, as in a mirror.

 

• Refraction (Option 2): The bending of light as it passes from one medium to another. Dispersion is a consequence of refraction, but the two are not the same.

 

• Diffraction (Option 4): The bending of light around the edges of an obstacle or a narrow slit.

question: Which of the following is the world's first DNA-based vaccine against COVID-19, developed in India?
solution_text:
The correct answer is ZyCoV-D.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• ZyCoV-D, developed by Zydus Cadila (Zydus Lifesciences) of Ahmedabad, is the world's first DNA plasmid-based vaccine against COVID-19 approved for human use. It received emergency use authorisation in India in August 2021. (जायकोव-डी — विश्व का पहला डीएनए आधारित कोविड टीका)

 

• Two features made it notable:
◦ It is administered by a needle-free applicator (jet injector), which reduces pain and the risk of injury.
◦ It was the first COVID-19 vaccine in India approved for the age group of 12 years and above.

 

• It was developed with support from the Department of Biotechnology under the Mission COVID Suraksha programme, and was given in a three-dose schedule.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Other COVID-19 vaccines associated with India:
◦ Covaxin (BBV152) — India's first indigenous vaccine, developed by Bharat Biotech with the ICMR and the National Institute of Virology, Pune; an inactivated virus vaccine
◦ Covishield — the Oxford-AstraZeneca viral vector vaccine, manufactured by the Serum Institute of India, Pune, the world's largest vaccine manufacturer by volume
◦ Corbevax — a protein subunit vaccine by Biological E
◦ iNCOVACC — the world's first intranasal COVID-19 vaccine, by Bharat Biotech

 

• India's vaccination drive began on 16 January 2021, and the CoWIN platform was used for registration and certification.

 

NOTE

 

• Covaxin (Option 2): An inactivated virus vaccine, not a DNA vaccine.

 

• Covishield (Option 3): A viral vector vaccine based on a chimpanzee adenovirus.

 

• Corbevax (Option 4): A protein subunit vaccine.

question: Which Indian city is popularly known as the 'Manchester of India'?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Ahmedabad.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Ahmedabad in Gujarat is popularly known as the "Manchester of India", because of the great concentration of cotton textile mills that grew up there from the nineteenth century onward. (अहमदाबाद — भारत का मैनचेस्टर)

 

• The comparison is with Manchester in England, the birthplace of the modern cotton industry. India's first cotton mill was set up at Bombay in 1854, and Ahmedabad's first at 1861 by Ranchhodlal Chhotalal.

 

• Ahmedabad is also called the "Manchester of the East", and the Sabarmati Ashram of Mahatma Gandhi is situated there. In 2017 it became India's first UNESCO World Heritage City.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Nicknames of Indian cities frequently asked in SSC:
◦ Manchester of South India — Coimbatore
◦ Manchester of North India — Kanpur; also called the Leather City of the World
◦ Silk City / Diamond City — Surat
◦ Queen of the Arabian Sea — Kochi (Cochin)
◦ Pink City — Jaipur; Blue City — Jodhpur; Golden City — Jaisalmer
◦ City of Lakes — Udaipur; City of Nawabs — Lucknow; City of Joy — Kolkata
◦ Garden City / Silicon Valley of India — Bengaluru
◦ Steel City — Jamshedpur; Gateway of India — Mumbai
◦ Scotland of the East — Shillong; Venice of the East — Alappuzha

 

NOTE

 

• Surat (Option 1): Known as the Silk City and the Diamond City of India.

 

• Kanpur (Option 2): The Manchester of North India, and a major centre of the leather industry.

 

• Coimbatore (Option 3): The Manchester of South India, a leading textile centre of Tamil Nadu.

question: Which state is the largest producer of zinc in India?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Rajasthan.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Rajasthan is by far the largest producer of zinc in India, and accounts for almost the whole of the country's output. (राजस्थान — जस्ता का सर्वाधिक उत्पादक)

 

• The principal zinc-lead deposits are at Zawar (near Udaipur), Rampura-Agucha (Bhilwara district, one of the largest zinc deposits in the world), Rajpura-Dariba and Sindesar Khurd. Hindustan Zinc Limited, with headquarters at Udaipur, is the main producer.

 

• The ore of zinc is zinc blende (sphalerite, ZnS), and zinc and lead usually occur together. The chief use of zinc is in galvanising iron and steel to prevent rusting; it is also used in making brass (copper + zinc) and in dry cells.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Leading mineral-producing states, frequently asked:
◦ Coal — Chhattisgarh, Odisha, Jharkhand
◦ Iron ore — Odisha, followed by Chhattisgarh and Karnataka
◦ Bauxite — Odisha; the ore of aluminium
◦ Manganese — Madhya Pradesh and Maharashtra
◦ Copper — Madhya Pradesh (Malanjkhand), Rajasthan (Khetri)
◦ Mica — Andhra Pradesh, Jharkhand, Rajasthan
◦ Gold — Karnataka (Kolar, Hutti)
◦ Limestone — Rajasthan and Madhya Pradesh
◦ Lignite — Tamil Nadu (Neyveli)

 

• The Indian Bureau of Mines, at Nagpur, publishes the Indian Minerals Yearbook.

 

NOTE

 

• Odisha (Option 2): The largest producer of iron ore, bauxite and chromite, but not of zinc.

 

• Jharkhand (Option 3): Rich in coal, iron ore, mica and copper.

 

• Andhra Pradesh (Option 4): Known for mica, barytes and limestone.

question: The Uber Cup, the world team championship for women in badminton, was first held in which year?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1957.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Uber Cup, the world team championship for women in badminton, was first held in 1957. (उबेर कप — 1957)

 

• It is named after Betty Uber, a distinguished English badminton player, who donated the trophy. The corresponding championship for men is the Thomas Cup, first held in 1948 and named after Sir George Alan Thomas.

 

• Both tournaments are organised by the Badminton World Federation (BWF) and are now held every two years, in even-numbered years, at the same venue.

 

• India won the Thomas Cup for the first time in 2022, defeating Indonesia in the final at Bangkok — a landmark achievement in Indian badminton.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Major badminton events: the All England Open, the BWF World Championships, the Sudirman Cup (mixed team) and the BWF World Tour Finals.

 

• Indian achievements: Prakash Padukone won the All England Championship in 1980 and Pullela Gopichand in 2001; Saina Nehwal won Olympic bronze at London 2012; P.V. Sindhu won silver at Rio 2016, bronze at Tokyo 2020 and became World Champion in 2019; Satwiksairaj Rankireddy and Chirag Shetty won the Asian Games gold in doubles in 2023.

 

• The BWF is headquartered at Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia.

 

NOTE

 

• 1948 (Option 1): The year of the first Thomas Cup, the men's team championship — the commonest confusion in this question.

 

• 1966 (Option 3) and 1972 (Option 4): Neither year is connected with the founding of the Uber Cup. Badminton became an official Olympic sport much later, at Barcelona in 1992.

question: The 'Make in India' initiative was launched by the Government of India in which year?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 2014.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The "Make in India" initiative was launched on 25 September 2014 by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, to encourage companies to manufacture their products in India and to make the country a global manufacturing hub. (मेक इन इंडिया — 2014)

 

• Its stated objectives were to raise the share of manufacturing in GDP to 25%, to create 100 million additional jobs, and to promote foreign direct investment, skill development and the ease of doing business.

 

• It covered 25 sectors at launch, including automobiles, textiles, pharmaceuticals, electronics, defence manufacturing, renewable energy and food processing. Its logo is a lion made of gears, symbolising strength and manufacture.

 

• Make in India 2.0 covers 27 sectors — 15 manufacturing and 12 service sectors — and is coordinated by the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT).

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Related initiatives and their years: Digital India (2015), Skill India (2015), Start-up India (2016), Atmanirbhar Bharat (2020) and the Production Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme (2020), which now covers 14 sectors.

 

• The National Manufacturing Policy, which first set the target of raising manufacturing to 25% of GDP and creating 100 million jobs, was announced in 2011, and provided for National Investment and Manufacturing Zones (NIMZs).

 

NOTE

 

• 2011 (Option 1): The year of the National Manufacturing Policy, which preceded Make in India and is often confused with it.

 

• 2016 (Option 3): The year Start-up India was launched.

 

• 2019 (Option 4): Not associated with the launch of any of these flagship manufacturing initiatives.

question: Who is the author of the novel 'The White Tiger', which won the Booker Prize in 2008?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Aravind Adiga.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "The White Tiger" (2008) was written by Aravind Adiga, and won the Man Booker Prize in 2008. It was his debut novel. (द व्हाइट टाइगर — अरविंद अडिगा)

 

• The novel is told as a series of letters written by Balram Halwai, a village boy who becomes a driver and then an entrepreneur, and it offers a sharp examination of class, corruption and the idea of the "Rooster Coop" in contemporary India.

 

• Adiga's other works include "Between the Assassinations", "Last Man in Tower", "Selection Day" and "Amnesty".

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Indian and Indian-origin winners of the Booker Prize:
◦ Salman Rushdie — *Midnight's Children* (1981); it also won the "Booker of Bookers"
◦ Arundhati Roy — *The God of Small Things* (1997)
◦ Kiran Desai — *The Inheritance of Loss* (2006)
◦ Aravind Adiga — *The White Tiger* (2008)
◦ Geetanjali Shree — *Tomb of Sand* (*Ret Samadhi*), International Booker Prize 2022, translated by Daisy Rockwell; the first book in any Indian language to win it
◦ Banu Mushtaq — *Heart Lamp*, International Booker Prize 2025, translated from Kannada by Deepa Bhasthi

 

• V.S. Naipaul won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 2001, and Rabindranath Tagore in 1913 for *Gitanjali*.

 

NOTE

 

• Kiran Desai (Option 2): Won the Booker in 2006 for *The Inheritance of Loss*.

 

• Amitav Ghosh (Option 3): Author of the Ibis Trilogy and the first Indian writer in English to receive the Jnanpith Award (2018).

 

• Vikas Swarup (Option 4): Author of "Q & A", on which the film *Slumdog Millionaire* was based.

question: A standard game of Water Polo consists of four quarters of how many minutes each?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 8.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• A standard game of Water Polo consists of four quarters of 8 minutes each, making 32 minutes of actual playing time. (वाटर पोलो — 4 क्वार्टर, प्रत्येक 8 मिनट)

 

• Each team has 7 players in the water — six field players and a goalkeeper — with six substitutes. A team must attempt a shot within 30 seconds of gaining possession.

 

• The game is played in a pool at least 2 metres deep, so that players cannot touch the bottom. Players may use only one hand to handle the ball, except the goalkeeper, who may use both.

 

• Water polo is governed by World Aquatics (formerly FINA) and was among the first team sports introduced at the Olympic Games, in 1900.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Duration of play in other sports, frequently asked together:
◦ Football — two halves of 45 minutes
◦ Hockey — four quarters of 15 minutes
◦ Basketball — four quarters of 10 minutes (FIBA) or 12 minutes (NBA)
◦ Handball — two halves of 30 minutes
◦ Kabaddi — two halves of 20 minutes
◦ Ice hockey — three periods of 20 minutes
◦ Rugby — two halves of 40 minutes

 

• Number of players in a team: Football 11, Hockey 11, Cricket 11, Basketball 5, Volleyball 6, Handball 7, Water Polo 7, Kabaddi 7, Kho-Kho 9 and Polo 4.

 

NOTE

 

• 6 minutes (Option 1), 10 minutes (Option 3) and 12 minutes (Option 4) are incorrect. Note that 10 and 12 minutes are the quarter lengths in basketball, which is the commonest confusion here.

question: Who is the author of the book 'Wise and Otherwise', a collection of real-life stories?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Sudha Murty.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Wise and Otherwise" (2002) was written by Sudha Murty. It is a collection of fifty-one real-life stories drawn from her travels across India and her experience of social work. (वाइज एंड अदरवाइज — सुधा मूर्ति)

 

• Sudha Murty is an author, educationist and philanthropist, and was Chairperson of the Infosys Foundation. She was the first woman engineer to be hired at TELCO (Tata Motors), after writing a postcard to J.R.D. Tata protesting against a "lady candidates need not apply" notice.

 

• Her other well-known works: "Dollar Bahu", "Mahashweta", "How I Taught My Grandmother to Read", "Three Thousand Stitches", "The Day I Stopped Drinking Milk" and the "Grandma's Bag of Stories" series for children.

 

• She was awarded the Padma Shri in 2006 and the Padma Bhushan in 2023, and was nominated to the Rajya Sabha in 2024.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Well-known Indian women writers and their works:
◦ Twinkle Khanna — *Mrs Funnybones*, *The Legend of Lakshmi Prasad*, *Pyjamas are Forgiving*
◦ Anita Desai — *Clear Light of Day*, *In Custody*, *Fire on the Mountain*; shortlisted for the Booker three times
◦ Shobhaa De — *Socialite Evenings*, *Starry Nights*
◦ Kiran Desai — *The Inheritance of Loss*
◦ Arundhati Roy — *The God of Small Things*
◦ Jhumpa Lahiri — *Interpreter of Maladies*, *The Namesake*, *In Other Words*
◦ Chitra Banerjee Divakaruni — *The Palace of Illusions*

 

NOTE

 

• Twinkle Khanna (Option 2): Author of "Mrs Funnybones" and "Welcome to Paradise".

 

• Anita Desai (Option 3): A distinguished novelist, thrice shortlisted for the Booker Prize.

 

• Shobhaa De (Option 4): A columnist and novelist known for her writing on urban Indian society.

question: The Department of Investment and Public Asset Management (DIPAM), which handles the disinvestment of Central Public Sector Enterprises, functions under which ministry?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Ministry of Finance.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Department of Investment and Public Asset Management (DIPAM) functions under the Ministry of Finance. (दीपम — वित्त मंत्रालय के अधीन)

 

• It was originally set up in 1999 as the Department of Disinvestment, became a separate ministry in 2001, was made a department of the Ministry of Finance again in 2004, and was renamed DIPAM in April 2016.

 

• Its mandate covers all matters relating to the management of the Central Government's investment in equity, including disinvestment, in Central Public Sector Enterprises.

 

• The disinvestment of CPSEs in India began in 1991-92, as part of the New Economic Policy. The Disinvestment Commission was set up in 1996 under the chairmanship of G.V. Ramakrishna.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Types of disinvestment: minority stake sale (government retains over 51% and control), majority stake sale, and strategic disinvestment, in which both ownership and management control are transferred to a private entity — as in the sale of Air India to the Tata Group in 2022.

 

• The New Public Sector Enterprise Policy (2021) classifies sectors as strategic — where a bare minimum of public enterprises will be retained — and non-strategic, where enterprises are to be privatised or closed.

 

• The Ministry of Finance has five departments: Economic Affairs, Expenditure, Revenue, DIPAM and Financial Services.

 

NOTE

 

• Ministry of Commerce and Industry (Option 2): Houses the DPIIT, which handles industrial policy and FDI, but not disinvestment.

 

• Ministry of Corporate Affairs (Option 3): Administers the Companies Act and the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code.

 

• Ministry of Heavy Industries (Option 4): Administers certain central public sector enterprises in the engineering sector, but does not manage disinvestment.

question: The Qutb Minar at Delhi, the tallest brick minaret in the world, has an approximate height of ______.
solution_text:
The correct answer is 72.5 metres.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Qutb Minar at Delhi is about 72.5 metres (nearly 238 feet) high, and is the tallest brick minaret in the world. (कुतुब मीनार — लगभग 72.5 मीटर)

 

• Its base diameter is about 14.3 metres and it tapers to about 2.7 metres at the top. It has five storeys, each marked by a projecting balcony, and a staircase of 379 steps.

 

• Its foundation was laid by Qutb-ud-din Aibak in 1199, and it was completed by Iltutmish, who added three storeys. The fifth storey was added by Firoz Shah Tughlaq, who repaired the minar after it was damaged by lightning. It is built of red sandstone and marble and was dedicated to the Sufi saint Qutbuddin Bakhtiyar Kaki.

 

• The Qutb Minar Complex was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1993, and includes the Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque, the Alai Darwaza built by Alauddin Khalji in 1311, the unfinished Alai Minar, and the Iron Pillar of Chandragupta II, famous for its resistance to rust.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Heights of other well-known Indian monuments:
◦ India Gate, New Delhi — about 42 metres
◦ Charminar, Hyderabad — about 56 metres
◦ Gateway of India, Mumbai — about 26 metres
◦ Statue of Unity, Gujarat — 182 metres, the tallest statue in the world
◦ Taj Mahal, Agra — about 73 metres including the dome and finial

 

NOTE

 

• 55 metres (Option 1) and 62 metres (Option 2) understate the height; 56 metres is close to the height of the Charminar.

 

• 85 metres (Option 4) overstates it. The figure to remember is 72.5 metres.

question: Which of the following is NOT a UNESCO World Heritage Site in India?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Charminar, Hyderabad.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Charminar at Hyderabad is not a UNESCO World Heritage Site. It is a monument of national importance protected by the Archaeological Survey of India, and it has been placed on India's tentative list, but it has not been inscribed. (चारमीनार — यूनेस्को विश्व धरोहर सूची में नहीं)

 

• It was built in 1591 by Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah, the fifth ruler of the Qutb Shahi dynasty, who also founded the city of Hyderabad.

 

• The other three options are all inscribed World Heritage Sites:
◦ Rani ki Vav, Patan (Gujarat) — inscribed in 2014; an eleventh-century stepwell built by Queen Udayamati, and depicted on the ₹100 currency note
◦ Great Living Chola Temples (Tamil Nadu) — inscribed in 1987; the Brihadeshwara Temple at Thanjavur, the temple at Gangaikondacholapuram and the Airavatesvara Temple at Darasuram
◦ Group of Monuments at Hampi (Karnataka) — inscribed in 1986; the capital of the Vijayanagara Empire

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• India's first World Heritage Sites, inscribed in 1983, were the Agra Fort, the Taj Mahal, the Ajanta Caves and the Ellora Caves.

 

• India's natural World Heritage Sites include Kaziranga, Keoladeo, Manas, Sundarbans, Nanda Devi and Valley of Flowers and the Western Ghats. Khangchendzonga National Park in Sikkim is India's only mixed site.

 

• India's World Heritage Cities are Ahmedabad (2017) and Jaipur (2019). Dholavira, a Harappan city in Gujarat, was inscribed in 2021, and the Sacred Ensembles of the Hoysalas in 2023.

 

NOTE

 

• Options 1, 2 and 4 are all UNESCO World Heritage Sites, inscribed in 2014, 1987 and 1986 respectively.

question: Who is regarded as the 'Father of Modern Chemistry'?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Antoine Lavoisier.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Antoine Laurent Lavoisier of France is regarded as the "Father of Modern Chemistry". (आधुनिक रसायन विज्ञान के जनक)

 

• His principal contributions:
◦ He established the Law of Conservation of Mass, which states that matter can neither be created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction.
◦ He disproved the phlogiston theory and demonstrated the true role of oxygen in combustion and respiration, and gave oxygen its name.
◦ He named hydrogen, and showed that water is a compound of hydrogen and oxygen.
◦ He introduced a systematic chemical nomenclature and wrote the "Traité Élémentaire de Chimie" (1789), the first modern textbook of chemistry.

 

• He was executed during the French Revolution in 1794.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Other founding figures of chemistry, frequently asked:
◦ John Dalton — the atomic theory (1808); called the Father of the Atomic Theory
◦ Robert Boyle — Boyle's Law; called the Father of Modern Chemistry by some older accounts, and the first to define an element in the modern sense
◦ Dmitri Mendeleev — the Periodic Table (1869); called the Father of the Periodic Table
◦ Friedrich Wöhler — synthesised urea from ammonium cyanate in 1828, disproving the theory of the "vital force" and founding organic chemistry
◦ Jöns Jacob Berzelius — introduced modern chemical symbols

 

• Fathers of other sciences: Physics — Galileo; Biology — Aristotle; Genetics — Gregor Mendel; Taxonomy — Carl Linnaeus; Ayurveda — Charaka; Surgery — Sushruta.

 

NOTE

 

• John Dalton (Option 2): Gave the atomic theory, but not the foundations of modern chemistry as a whole.

 

• Robert Boyle (Option 3): A pioneer of experimental chemistry and the author of *The Sceptical Chymist*.

 

• Dmitri Mendeleev (Option 4): Devised the Periodic Table and predicted undiscovered elements.

question: Which element was predicted by Dmitri Mendeleev under the name 'Eka-Aluminium'?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Gallium.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Mendeleev left gaps in his periodic table for elements not yet discovered, and named them using the Sanskrit prefix "Eka", meaning one — that is, one place below a known element. (एका-एल्युमिनियम — गैलियम)

 

• His three famous predictions and the elements that filled them:
◦ Eka-Aluminium → Gallium, discovered by Lecoq de Boisbaudran in 1875
◦ Eka-Boron → Scandium, discovered by Lars Nilson in 1879
◦ Eka-Silicon → Germanium, discovered by Clemens Winkler in 1886

 

• In each case the properties of the newly discovered element agreed closely with those Mendeleev had predicted, and this was the greatest triumph of his periodic table.

 

• Mendeleev's Periodic Law (1869) stated that the properties of elements are a periodic function of their atomic masses. He arranged the 63 elements then known in eight groups and six periods.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Limitations of Mendeleev's table: no fixed position for hydrogen, which resembles both alkali metals and halogens; isotopes could not be placed; and certain pairs appeared in anomalous order — cobalt (58.9) before nickel (58.7), and tellurium before iodine.

 

• The Modern Periodic Law, given by Henry Moseley in 1913, states that the properties of elements are a periodic function of their atomic numbers. The modern table has 18 groups and 7 periods.

 

• Earlier attempts at classification: Dobereiner's Law of Triads (1817) and Newlands' Law of Octaves (1866).

 

NOTE

 

• Scandium (Option 2): Predicted by Mendeleev as Eka-Boron.

 

• Germanium (Option 3): Predicted as Eka-Silicon.

 

• Titanium (Option 4): Already known in Mendeleev's time and duly placed in his table; it was not one of the predicted elements.

question: Who was the first Home Minister of independent India?

solution_text:
The correct answer is Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel was the first Home Minister of independent India, and also the first Deputy Prime Minister, in the Cabinet formed on 15 August 1947. (सरदार पटेल — स्वतंत्र भारत के प्रथम गृह मंत्री)

 

• As Home Minister he held the portfolios of Home Affairs, Information and Broadcasting, and States, and it was in the last of these that he carried out his greatest work — the integration of over 560 princely states into the Indian Union, assisted by V.P. Menon. For this he is called the "Iron Man of India" and the "Bismarck of India".

 

• He founded the Indian Administrative Service and is therefore also known as the patron saint of India's civil servants. His birthday, 31 October, is observed as Rashtriya Ekta Diwas (National Unity Day), and the Statue of Unity in Gujarat, the tallest statue in the world at 182 metres, was dedicated to him in 2018. He was awarded the Bharat Ratna posthumously in 1991.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The first Cabinet of independent India and its principal members:
◦ Prime Minister and External Affairs — Jawaharlal Nehru
◦ Deputy Prime Minister and Home — Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel
◦ Defence — Baldev Singh
◦ Finance — R.K. Shanmukham Chetty
◦ Law — Dr. B.R. Ambedkar
◦ Education — Maulana Abul Kalam Azad
◦ Health — Rajkumari Amrit Kaur, the first woman Cabinet Minister
◦ Industry and Supplies — Dr. Syama Prasad Mookerjee
◦ Railways — John Mathai

 

• Dr. Rajendra Prasad became the first President of India, and C. Rajagopalachari the last Governor-General.

 

NOTE

 

• Maulana Abul Kalam Azad (Option 1): The first Education Minister of independent India.

 

• Dr. Rajendra Prasad (Option 2): Minister of Food and Agriculture in the first Cabinet, and later the first President of India.

 

• C. Rajagopalachari (Option 3): The last Governor-General of India (1948-1950) and later Home Minister, but not the first.
